1.note: Isaiah is using the term **Behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Look]

Here, **hand** represents the power/control/capability of a Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh’s power]

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative phrase **too short**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [Yahweh’s hand is strong enough to save]

Isaiah is using **is not too short to save** as a common expression of the culture to mean that Yahweh does not lack the power to save. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [does not lack the power to save]

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative word **too heavy**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [and his ear is able to hear]

Isaiah is using **his ear not too heavy to hear** as a common expression of the culture to mean that Yahweh is not unwilling or unable to hear. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he is not unable to hear you]

2.note: Isaiah uses the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between what Yahweh is able to do and what keeps him from saving the people. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Instead,]

2.q: עֲוֺנֹֽתֵי⁠כֶם֙ הָי֣וּ מַבְדִּלִ֔ים בֵּינֵ⁠כֶ֕ם לְ⁠בֵ֖ין אֱלֹֽהֵי⁠כֶ֑ם וְ⁠חַטֹּֽאותֵי⁠כֶ֗ם הִסְתִּ֧ירוּ פָנִ֛ים מִ⁠כֶּ֖ם
2.note:
The words **you** and **your** are plural because Isaiah is addressing the Israelites as a group. Those words are plural in the next verse for the same reason.
So use plural forms in your translation if your language marks that distinction.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquities**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the wicked things you have done]

Here, **face** represents a person’s attention and favor. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [have caused him to ignore you]

3.note: The expression **are stained** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [blood stains your palms]

Here, **blood** represents guilt regarding the violence and killing that the people have committed. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [your palms are stained with the guilt of violence]

Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and your fingers are stained with iniquity] or [and iniquity stains your fingers]
Here, **lips** represent the act of speaking. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [You have spoken falsehood]

Here, **tongue** represents the act of speaking. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [you murmur wickedness when you speak]

4.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for what is right]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **emptiness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [trusting in what is worthless]

Here Isaiah is speaking of the people planning and carrying out evil as if evil were a child that they were **conceiving** and **birthing**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [planning trouble and carrying out iniquity]

5.q: בֵּיצֵ֤י צִפְעוֹנִי֙ בִּקֵּ֔עוּ וְ⁠קוּרֵ֥י עַכָּבִ֖ישׁ יֶאֱרֹ֑גוּ
5.note: Here Isaiah is speaking of the deadly and worthless schemes that the people make as if they were **the eggs of a viper** and **the webs of a spider**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They devise deadly schemes, and they develop worthless schemes]

The expression **is crushed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [when someone crushes an egg]

6.q: קֽוּרֵי⁠הֶם֙ לֹא יִהְי֣וּ לְ⁠בֶ֔גֶד וְ⁠לֹ֥א יִתְכַּסּ֖וּ בְּ⁠מַֽעֲשֵׂי⁠הֶ֑ם
6.note: Here Isaiah is speaking of the people’s deeds as if they were spider **webs** that could never become **clothing** to cover anyone. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Their deeds are as useless as spider webs, which can never provide clothing to cover anyone]

Isaiah is using the possessive form to describe **works** that are characterized by **iniquity**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [are wicked works]

Here, **in their palms** represents carrying out an action. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and they do deeds of violence]

7.note: Isaiah is using **feet** to represent the whole person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They run to evil]

Here, **innocent blood** represents the murder of innocent people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to kill innocent people]

8.note: Here Isaiah is speaking of a peaceful manner of living as if it were a **way**, or road, that a person could travel. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [how to live in peace]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **justice**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and they do not do what is just]

Here Isaiah is speaking of the people’s dishonest conduct as if they had made the **paths** they walk on **crooked**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They have made for themselves a dishonest way of life]

9.note: Isaiah uses the word **Therefore** to indicate that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [As a result,]

9.q: רָחַ֤ק מִשְׁפָּט֙ מִמֶּ֔⁠נּוּ וְ⁠לֹ֥א תַשִּׂיגֵ֖⁠נוּ צְדָקָ֑ה
9.note: Isaiah is speaking of two abstract nouns, **justice** and **righteousness**, as if they were living beings that could stay far away and fail to catch up with the people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [we do not receive what is just, and we do not experience what is right]

By **us**, Isaiah means to include both himself and those to whom he is speaking, so use the inclusive form of that word if your language marks that distinction. Alternate translation: [justice is far from us, the people of Israel]

9.q: נְקַוֶּ֤ה לָ⁠אוֹר֙ וְ⁠הִנֵּה חֹ֔שֶׁךְ לִ⁠נְגֹה֖וֹת בָּ⁠אֲפֵל֥וֹת נְהַלֵּֽךְ
9.note: Here Isaiah is speaking of deliverance and well-being as if they were **light** and **brightness**, and of trouble and distress as if they were **darkness** and **gloom**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [We wait for deliverance, but behold, distress; for well-being, we experience trouble]

9.q: נְקַוֶּ֤ה לָ⁠אוֹר֙ וְ⁠הִנֵּה־חֹ֔שֶׁךְ לִ⁠נְגֹה֖וֹת בָּ⁠אֲפֵל֥וֹת נְהַלֵּֽךְ
9.note: Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [We wait for light, but behold, darkness; we wait for brightness, but we walk in gloom]

Isaiah is using the term **behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [but instead there is darkness]

10.q: נְגַֽשְׁשָׁ֤ה כַֽ⁠עִוְרִים֙ קִ֔יר וּ⁠כְ⁠אֵ֥ין עֵינַ֖יִם נְגַשֵּׁ֑שָׁה
10.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **the blind** must grope along a wall because they cannot see, so the people **grope** because they do not know what they should do. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [We do not know what we should do; we feel along the wall like people who are blind, and we grope about like people who have no eyes]

Isaiah is using the adjective **blind** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [like blind people]

The point of this comparison is that just as a person stumbles in the dimness of **twilight**, so the people stumble even at **noon**, when it is fully light. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [We stumble at noon, when it is fully light, as easily as a person stumbles in the dimness of twilight]

The point of this comparison is that just as **ones having died** have no strength, so the people are helpless even **among the strong**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [among the strong, we are as powerless as those who have died]

Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [among people who are strong we are like ones who have died]

11.q: נֶהֱמֶ֤ה כַ⁠דֻּבִּים֙ כֻּלָּ֔⁠נוּ וְ⁠כַ⁠יּוֹנִ֖ים הָגֹ֣ה נֶהְגֶּ֑ה
11.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **bears growl** and **doves murmur**, so the people groan and mourn over their distress. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [We all groan over our distress as bears growl, and we mourn as doves murmur]

Isaiah uses the word **but** here to indicate a contrast between **We wait** and **there is none**. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Although we wait for justice, there is no justice] or [Although we wait for justice, justice does not come]

Here Isaiah is speaking of **salvation** as if **it** were an object located **far** away from the people. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for salvation, but we are not saved]

Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. He means that we wait **for salvation**. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [we wait to be saved, but salvation is far from us]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for someone to save us]

12.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **transgressions**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the wrong things we have done]

The pronoun **it** refers to the people’s **sins**, spoken of together as a single group. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and our sins, as a group, testify against us]

Isaiah is speaking of the people’s **sins** as if they were a living witness who **testifies against** them in court. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and our sins reveal our guilt]
The word **you** is singular here because it refers to Yahweh. So use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

13.note: Here Isaiah is speaking of abandoning God as if that were physically **turning away from** following him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and abandoning our God]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **oppression** and **revolt**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [about oppressing others and rebelling against God]

Here Isaiah is speaking of the people devising deceit as if they were **conceiving** a child. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [planning and uttering words of falsehood]

Here Isaiah is speaking of the inner mind, where a conceives of and develops ideas and plans, as if it were the physical **heart**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in the mind]

14.q: וְ⁠הֻסַּ֤ג אָחוֹר֙ מִשְׁפָּ֔ט וּ⁠צְדָקָ֖ה מֵ⁠רָח֣וֹק תַּעֲמֹ֑ד
14.note: Isaiah is speaking of **justice** and **righteousness** as if they were persons who could be **driven back** and made to stand **from faraway**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And there is no justice anywhere, and righteous behavior is nowhere to be found]

The expression **is driven back** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And people drive justice back]

14.q: כָשְׁלָ֤ה בָֽ⁠רְחוֹב֙ אֱמֶ֔ת וּ⁠נְכֹחָ֖ה לֹא תוּכַ֥ל לָ⁠בֽוֹא
14.note: Isaiah is speaking of **truth** and **uprightness** as if they were persons who could stumble and not be **able to enter** a place. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [there is no truth in the public square, and honesty is nowhere to be found]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **uprightness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and what is upright]

15.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **truth**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [no one speaks truthfully]

Here Isaiah is speaking of a person who stops doing evil as if he were **turning** away from it, and of that person being victimized as if he were **plunder** that others seize. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and whoever stops doing evil becomes a victim]

Isaiah is not referring to a specific person by the phrase **the one turning from evil**. He means anyone who turns from evil, in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and anyone who turns from evil]

Isaiah is using **it was evil in his eyes** as a common expression of the culture to mean that in Yahweh’s judgment it was evil. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he considered it evil]

16.note: Here, **his arm** represents Yahweh’s own power and strength. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [So his own power brought him salvation]

The repeated pronoun **it, it** refers to Yahweh’s **righteousness** and emphasizes that his righteousness was what supported him. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and his righteousness was the very thing that supported him]

Isaiah is speaking of Yahweh’s **righteousness** as if it were a living thing that could support him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and because he was righteous, he sustained himself] or [and Yahweh’s righteous actions supported him]

17.q: וַ⁠יִּלְבַּ֤שׁ צְדָקָה֙ כַּ⁠שִּׁרְיָ֔ן וְ⁠כ֥וֹבַע יְשׁוּעָ֖ה בְּ⁠רֹאשׁ֑⁠וֹ
17.note: Here Isaiah is speaking of Yahweh’s **righteousness** and **salvation** as if they were a **breastplate** and a **helmet** that he put on like a warrior preparing for battle. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And his righteous acts protected him like a breastplate, and his power to save protected him like a helmet on his head]

17.q: וַ⁠יִּלְבַּ֞שׁ בִּגְדֵ֤י נָקָם֙ תִּלְבֹּ֔שֶׁת וַ⁠יַּ֥עַט כַּ⁠מְעִ֖יל קִנְאָֽה
17.note: Here Isaiah is speaking of Yahweh’s **vengeance** and **zeal** as if they were **garments** and a **robe** that he wore as **clothing**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he was determined to take vengeance, and he was intensely zealous]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **vengeance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [garments for avenging himself]

18.note: Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [he will give heat to his adversaries, he will give recompense to his enemies]

Here Isaiah is speaking of Yahweh’s fierce anger as if it were **heat** that he directs toward his adversaries. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [fierce anger to his adversaries]
See how you translated the term “coastlands” in 40:15. Alternate translation: [to the people of all lands]

19.q: וְ⁠יִֽירְא֤וּ מִֽ⁠מַּעֲרָב֙ אֶת־שֵׁ֣ם יְהוָ֔ה וּ⁠מִ⁠מִּזְרַח־שֶׁ֖מֶשׁ אֶת־כְּבוֹד֑⁠וֹ
19.note: The pronoun **they** refers to people throughout the world, in both the distant west and the distant east. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And people everywhere will fear the name and glory of Yahweh]
Here, **the name of Yahweh** represents Yahweh himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh himself]

Isaiah is referring to the whole earth by naming two major regions, **the setting** of the sun in the west and **the rising of the sun** in the east. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [everywhere on the earth, and his glory everywhere on the earth]

Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and they will fear his glory from the rising of the sun]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a narrow stream** driven by the wind rushes powerfully, so Yahweh will come with great power and force. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [he will come with great force, rushing like a narrow stream]

20.note: Here, **Zion** represents the people who live there. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to the people of Zion]

Here Isaiah is speaking of people who repent as if they were physically **turning** away **from transgression**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and to the ones who repent of their sins]

Here, **Jacob** represents the descendants of the man Jacob, that is, the people of Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [among the people of Israel]

21.note: The pronoun **them** refers to the people whom Yahweh will redeem. In the next clause, Yahweh addresses these same people directly as **you**. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the people whom I will redeem]

Isaiah is using **says Yahweh** to indicate that what has been said is a direct quotation from Yahweh and comes with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

Yahweh is using **put in your mouth** as a common expression of the culture to mean that he has given his people a message to speak. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [which I have given you to speak]

This could mean: (1) a message the people are to speak on behalf of Yahweh. Alternate translation, as in the UST: [and the message that I have given you to speak] or (2) the terms of the covenant, which the people are to repeat to ratify it. Alternate translation: [the terms of this covenant, which you are to repeat]

Here, **your mouth** represents the words that you speak. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [will not depart from the words you speak]

Here Yahweh is speaking of descendants as if they were **seed** that a person produces. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [or from the mouth of your descendants or from the mouth of your descendants’ descendants]
